name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q01 - Sequence of establishing liquid vapour equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following experimental steps in the correct chronological sequence for measuring the equilibrium vapour pressure of water at a constant temperature using a closed box fitted with a mercury manometer:

(i) Water vapour pressure rises, increasing the rate of condensation over time.
(ii) Anhydrous calcium chloride removes moisture from the closed box and is tilted aside.
(iii) Rate of evaporation equals rate of condensation, and the mercury level becomes constant.
(iv) A watch glass containing liquid water is quickly placed inside the dry box.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Liquid-vapour equilibrium is attained in a closed system when the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation at a constant temperature.

Step 2: Chronological Ordering
First, anhydrous calcium chloride dries the air inside the closed box and is moved aside. Next, a watch glass containing water is placed inside the dry box, initiating evaporation at a constant rate. As water vapour accumulates, the pressure inside the box rises and the rate of condensation increases with time. Finally, the rate of condensation becomes equal to the rate of evaporation, and the mercury level in the manometer stabilizes at a constant value.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is (ii) → (iv) → (i) → (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q02 - Steps for calculating equilibrium concentrations

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct logical sequence to calculate equilibrium concentrations from known initial concentrations:

(i) Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the \(K_c\) expression and solve for \(x\).
(ii) Write the balanced chemical equation for the reversible reaction.
(iii) Verify the calculated concentrations by substituting them back into the \(K_c\) expression.
(iv) Construct a table listing initial concentrations, changes in terms of \(x\), and equilibrium concentrations.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Solving for equilibrium concentrations requires reaction stoichiometry, mass balance from initial conditions, and the equilibrium law.

Step 2: Logical Ordering
First, write the balanced chemical equation to establish stoichiometric coefficients. Second, construct a table under the balanced equation showing initial concentrations, changes in concentration in terms of \(x\), and equilibrium concentrations. Third, substitute these equilibrium expressions into the \(K_c\) equation and solve for \(x\) (choosing the chemically meaningful root). Finally, compute the equilibrium concentrations and verify them by substituting back into the \(K_c\) expression.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical sequence is (ii) → (iv) → (i) → (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q03 - Increasing order of acid strength across period

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following hydrides of second-period elements in the increasing order of their acid strength:

(i) \(\mathrm{HF}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{CH}_4\)
(iv) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When comparing elements in the same row (period) of the periodic table, the polarity of the \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond is the deciding factor for acid strength.

Step 2: Ordering Analysis
Across the second period from carbon to fluorine (\(\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{N}, \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{F}\)), the electronegativity of atom \(\mathrm{A}\) increases. As electronegativity increases, the \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond becomes more polar, making proton loss easier and increasing acid strength: \(\mathrm{CH}_4 < \mathrm{NH}_3 < \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} < \mathrm{HF}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of acid strength is (iii) → (ii) → (iv) → (i).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q04 - Decreasing order of acid strength of hydrogen halides

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following hydrogen halides in the decreasing order of their acid strength in aqueous solution (strongest to weakest):

(i) \(\mathrm{HCl}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{HI}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{HF}\)
(iv) \(\mathrm{HBr}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When comparing elements in the same group of the periodic table, \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond strength is more important than bond polarity in determining acid strength.

Step 2: Ordering Analysis
Down Group 17 from \(\mathrm{F}\) to \(\mathrm{I}\), atomic size increases, which decreases the \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{X}\) bond strength. Weaker \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{X}\) bonds dissociate more readily, so acid strength increases down the group: \(\mathrm{HF} \ll \mathrm{HCl} \ll \mathrm{HBr} \ll \mathrm{HI}\). In decreasing order (strongest to weakest), the sequence is \(\mathrm{HI} > \mathrm{HBr} > \mathrm{HCl} > \mathrm{HF}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of acid strength is (ii) → (iv) → (i) → (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q05 - Increasing order of pH of salt and acid solutions

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following \(0.1\;\mathrm{M}\) aqueous solutions at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) in the increasing order of their \(\mathrm{pH}\):

(i) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{HCl}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\)
(iv) \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Strong acids have very low \(\mathrm{pH}\), salts of strong acid and weak base hydrolyse to give \(\mathrm{pH} < 7\), salts of strong acid and strong base are neutral (\(\mathrm{pH} = 7\)), and salts of weak acid and strong base hydrolyse to give \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\).

Step 2: Ordering Analysis
\(0.1\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\) is a strong acid with \(\mathrm{pH} = 1\). \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\) undergoes cationic hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) to produce \(\mathrm{H}^+\), giving an acidic solution with \(\mathrm{pH} < 7\) (higher than \(0.1\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\)). \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) does not hydrolyse and has \(\mathrm{pH} = 7\). \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\) undergoes anionic hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-\) to produce \(\mathrm{OH}^-\), giving a basic solution with \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of \(\mathrm{pH}\) is (ii) → (iv) → (i) → (iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q06 - Increasing order of pKa of weak acids

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following weak acids at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) in the increasing order of their \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) values:

(i) Acetic acid (\(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\))
(ii) Hydrocyanic acid (\(K_a = 4.9 \times 10^{-10}\))
(iii) Nitrous acid (\(K_a = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}\))
(iv) Hypochlorous acid (\(K_a = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(K_a\) values at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\): \(\mathrm{HNO}_2 = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}\), \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\), \(\mathrm{HClO} = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\), \(\mathrm{HCN} = 4.9 \times 10^{-10}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log K_a\), so \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) increases as \(K_a\) decreases.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stronger weak acids have larger \(K_a\) and smaller \(\mathrm{p}K_a\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Ordering the acids from largest \(K_a\) to smallest \(K_a\) gives: \(\mathrm{HNO}_2\) (\(4.5 \times 10^{-4}\)) > \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) (\(1.74 \times 10^{-5}\)) > \(\mathrm{HClO}\) (\(3.0 \times 10^{-8}\)) > \(\mathrm{HCN}\) (\(4.9 \times 10^{-10}\)). Because \(\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log K_a\), this corresponds to increasing \(\mathrm{p}K_a\): \(\mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{HNO}_2) \approx 3.35 < \mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}) \approx 4.76 < \mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{HClO}) \approx 7.52 < \mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{HCN}) \approx 9.31\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct increasing order of \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) is (iii) → (i) → (iv) → (ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_SEQ_Q07 - Isotope scrambling experiment demonstrating dynamic equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological sequence for the deuterium isotope experiment demonstrating the dynamic nature of chemical equilibrium in Haber's synthesis of ammonia:

(i) Mass spectrometric analysis detects \(\mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{NH}_2\mathrm{D}, \mathrm{NHD}_2, \mathrm{ND}_3\) as well as \(\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{HD}, \mathrm{D}_2\).
(ii) Two equilibrium mixtures—one containing \(\mathrm{N}_2, \mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{NH}_3\) and the other containing \(\mathrm{N}_2, \mathrm{D}_2, \mathrm{ND}_3\)—are prepared under identical temperature and partial pressure conditions.
(iii) Analysis shows that the total concentration of ammonia remains unchanged.
(iv) The two equilibrium mixtures are mixed together and left for some time.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Scrambling of \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{D}\) isotopes without any change in total ammonia concentration proves that forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates at equilibrium.

Step 2: Chronological Ordering
First, two separate equilibrium mixtures—one prepared with \(\mathrm{H}_2\) and the other with \(\mathrm{D}_2\) under identical conditions—reach the same equilibrium composition. Second, the two equilibrium mixtures are combined and left for a while. Third, chemical analysis confirms that the total concentration of ammonia remains identical to before. Finally, mass spectrometric analysis reveals all mixed isotopologues (\(\mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{NH}_2\mathrm{D}, \mathrm{NHD}_2, \mathrm{ND}_3\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{HD}, \mathrm{D}_2\)), proving continuous forward and reverse reactions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is (ii) → (iv) → (iii) → (i).
